heading: Stronger splits into separate measurements
narration: A tensile test, described in standard methods published by ASTM International, takes a specimen shaped a little like a dog bone, grips both ends, and stretches it while recording force and extension.

heading: Stronger splits into separate measurements

heading: Stronger splits into separate measurements
narration: The steep straight section at the start gives stiffness, the elastic modulus: how hard the material resists stretching before it springs back.

heading: Stronger splits into separate measurements
narration: The point where that line bends over gives yield strength, the stress at which the material begins to deform permanently.

args.meaning: the stress at which the material begins to deform permanently

heading: Stronger splits into separate measurements
narration: The peak of the curve gives ultimate tensile strength, the most stress it carries before it narrows and tears.

heading: Stronger splits into separate measurements
narration: Yield strength is not the same as stiffness. A material can be stiff and weak, or flexible and strong.

heading: Steel wins a same-size fight
narration: Start with the property that is least ambiguous. Stiffness barely changes with alloying or heat treatment, which makes it the cleanest comparison.

heading: Steel wins a same-size fight
narration: ASM International reference data put the elastic modulus of steel at about 200 gigapascals and aluminum at about 70.

narration: No heat treatment fixes that, because stiffness is set largely by the bonding between atoms, not by the microstructure that processing controls.

heading: Equal weight flips the bending contest
narration: Now divide each stiffness by its density. At equal size, steel is nearly three times stiffer, but it is also nearly three times as dense, so the two ratios land almost on top of each other.

heading: Equal weight flips the bending contest
narration: Steel is not meaningfully stiffer per kilogram. Where aluminum pulls ahead is in bending.

heading: Equal weight flips the bending contest
narration: Allowed the same weight of metal, aluminum gives you roughly three times the volume, so you can make a plate thicker or a tube wider.

heading: Equal weight flips the bending contest
narration: Bending stiffness grows far faster than thickness does, so a thicker aluminum panel of equal weight can be considerably stiffer than the thin steel one it replaces.

heading: Equal weight flips the bending contest
narration: That is a large part of why aircraft skins, bicycle frames and some car body panels use aluminum. The metal is not stiffer. The geometry it allows is.

heading: Alloying moves aluminum past ordinary steel
narration: Strength is where processing matters, and where the answer changes. Pure aluminum is soft.

args.caption: Minimum yield strength required by the ASTM A36 standard

heading: Alloying moves aluminum past ordinary steel
narration: A thin strip bends easily in your fingers, and the pure metal is used where conductivity or corrosion resistance matters more than load.

heading: Alloying moves aluminum past ordinary steel
narration: Aluminum alloys are a different material. Adding small amounts of elements such as copper, magnesium, silicon or zinc, then heat treating the metal, can multiply its strength many times over.

args.caption: Minimum yield strength required by the ASTM A36 standard

heading: Alloying moves aluminum past ordinary steel
narration: The everyday structural steel used in buildings, specified under the ASTM A36 standard, must have a yield strength of at least 250 megapascals.

heading: Alloying moves aluminum past ordinary steel
narration: Common heat-treated aluminum alloys, such as 6061 in the T6 temper, are listed in ASM International data with a typical yield strength above that minimum. The aerospace alloy 7075, heat treated, goes considerably further.

args.caption: Minimum yield strength required by the ASTM A36 standard

heading: Alloying moves aluminum past ordinary steel
narration: Metallurgists know what causes that jump because they can see it. Electron microscopes resolve particles far too small for any optical instrument, and comparisons between the same alloy in different heat-treated states link particle size and spacing to measured strength.

args.meaning: strengthening by tiny particles that form inside the grains during heat treatment

heading: Alloying moves aluminum past ordinary steel
narration: The process is called precipitation hardening: strengthening by tiny particles that form inside the grains during heat treatment.

heading: Alloying moves aluminum past ordinary steel
narration: Those particles obstruct dislocations, the line defects whose sliding is how metals deform permanently.

args.meaning: strengthening by tiny particles that form inside the grains during heat treatment

heading: Alloying moves aluminum past ordinary steel
narration: The mechanism has an edge. Heat the alloy too much, or for too long, and the particles grow and coarsen, spacing out until dislocations slip between them and the strength falls away.

heading: The strongest steels stay out of reach
narration: But steel has heat treatments of its own, and they go further.

heading: Fatigue and heat expose what a tensile test misses
narration: A tensile test pulls once. Real structures are loaded thousands or millions of times, and here the two metals behave differently in a way a single strength figure hides.

heading: Fatigue and heat expose what a tensile test misses
narration: Many steels show what is called an endurance limit: below a certain stress, they survive an effectively unlimited number of cycles in testing.

heading: Fatigue and heat expose what a tensile test misses
narration: Aluminum alloys generally do not show a clear one. Keep cycling them, even at modest stress, and fatigue cracks can eventually start.

heading: Fatigue and heat expose what a tensile test misses
narration: ASM International's fatigue literature treats this as a central design difference, and it is why aluminum aircraft structures are inspected on schedules rather than assumed to last indefinitely.

heading: Fatigue and heat expose what a tensile test misses
narration: Temperature is the other gap. Aluminum melts at about 660 degrees Celsius, far below steel, and its alloys lose much of their strength well before that point.

heading: Fatigue and heat expose what a tensile test misses
narration: Steel keeps useful strength to higher temperatures, which is one reason it remains the default for many structures that must survive heat.

heading: Aluminum seals itself while steel rusts through
narration: One more property often gets folded into the word strong, and it deserves separating.

includes: a thin film of aluminum oxide

heading: Aluminum seals itself while steel rusts through
narration: Freshly cut aluminum reacts with oxygen almost immediately, forming a thin film of aluminum oxide that clings to the surface and slows further attack.

heading: Aluminum seals itself while steel rusts through
narration: Plain carbon steel forms rust instead, an oxide that flakes away and exposes fresh metal beneath.

includes: a thin film of aluminum oxide

heading: Aluminum seals itself while steel rusts through
narration: That is why an unpainted aluminum window frame can last for decades, while unprotected mild steel needs paint, galvanizing, or a different alloy such as stainless steel.

heading: Aluminum seals itself while steel rusts through
narration: It is not a difference in strength at all, but over a structure's life it can decide which metal is still carrying load.

includes: a thin film of aluminum oxide

heading: Aluminum seals itself while steel rusts through
narration: Aluminum is not immune either. Some high-strength alloys, especially those containing copper, corrode more readily and are often clad with a layer of purer aluminum for that reason.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: When you see this comparison in an article or an advertisement, notice what is being held constant.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: A chart that puts aluminum and steel side by side has already made choices: which alloy, which property, and whether it compares at equal size or equal weight.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Notice too which steel it chose. A strong aluminum alloy set beside mild steel tells one story.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: The same alloy set beside a quenched and tempered high-strength steel tells the opposite one.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Neither chart is lying. Each one answers a narrower question than its headline admits.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: These figures describe test specimens under controlled conditions, not finished parts. A handbook value for an alloy is a typical or minimum figure drawn from many tests, and an individual batch can sit above or below it.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Real components carry welds, holes, scratches and stresses locked in during manufacturing, and welding in particular can soften heat-treated aluminum near the joint.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: None of the numbers here tell you whether a particular bicycle, ladder or car is safe, and none of them rank the two metals for a specific job.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: That ranking comes from design calculation, safety margins and testing of the actual part, which is a separate body of evidence from the material data.

heading: Closing
narration: So steel is usually the stronger and stiffer metal at equal size, and aluminum is the one that can make a structure lighter for the load it carries.

heading: Closing
narration: The comparison only means something once you say what you are holding equal.

heading: Closing
narration: The metal does not answer the question. The question you ask it does.
